analysis.one_liner: Bans data brokers from selling people's health and location data.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 4 senators, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for data brokers to sell, license, or transfer data showing where a person has been or what their health condition is — including health questions typed into AI chatbots. The Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and individuals could all sue violators, with penalties up to 15% of a company's parent company's annual revenue. The FTC would also get $1 billion to enforce the new rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose phone or health information is currently bought and sold: the bill cuts off data brokers' ability to profit from people's location history and health conditions, including pregnancies, disabilities, and mental health, and gives people and state enforcers tools to force deletion of improperly sold data and recover damages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone whose health or location data is sold

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for a data broker to sell, license, trade, transfer, or share location data or health data about an individual, whether that data was stated directly or inferred — including health questions entered into AI systems.
Also makes it unlawful for any company to feed location or health data to a data broker, cutting off the supply, not just the resale.

Lets the FTC enforce the ban as an unfair or deceptive practice, sue in court for civil penalties, damages, restitution, and orders to delete the data — and explicitly covers nonprofits, which the FTC normally cannot police.

Gives every state attorney general power to sue violators on behalf of residents, and gives individuals their own right to sue for injunctions, damages, deletion of data, and attorney's fees, with a 6-year window from when they learn of the violation.
Sets a civil penalty of up to 15% of the violator's ultimate parent entity's revenue from the prior 12 months, so large corporate parents cannot shield themselves behind subsidiaries.
Appropriates $1 billion to the FTC, available through 2035, to fund enforcement.
Preserves normal medical handling by exempting HIPAA-compliant actions by covered entities and business associates, newsworthy publication, and disclosures the individual validly authorized.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the app and adtech companies that supply them lose a lucrative trade in location and health information. Taxpayers fund the $1 billion FTC appropriation. Legitimate uses — HIPAA-compliant health care operations, journalism, and disclosures people actually authorize — are exempted.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and adtech data sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill carries a $1 billion appropriation to the FTC on top of its existing budget, a real cost to taxpayers.

The penalty structure is steep: up to 15% of a parent company's entire annual revenue per violation, combined with a broad private right of action that any 'affected' person can invoke, which businesses would argue invites heavy litigation beyond pure data brokers.

The HIPAA carve-out leaves a channel open: a broker acting as a HIPAA business associate or covered entity can still handle health information so long as it stays within HIPAA's rules, so not all health-data trafficking is cut off.

The ban cannot take effect until the FTC completes rulemaking — including a rule defining the term 'data' — within 180 days of enactment, so enforcement would lag and key definitions would be left to regulators to fight over.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and concrete: health conditions and physical movements are among the most sensitive data about a person, and the bill would shut down their commercial resale with real enforcement teeth and funding. The costs — $1 billion in appropriations, litigation risk from the broad private right of action, and steep revenue-based penalties — are meaningful but the kind of tradeoff an honest supporter would accept; the HIPAA carve-out and reliance on FTC rulemaking are the weakest design points.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it so far.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 13, 2026, joined on introduction by Sens. Sanders, Whitehouse, and Wyden.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; that remains the last action of record.
Four senators cosponsored the bill: 3 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents.

The bill text bans brokers from selling location and health data, empowers the FTC, state attorneys general, and private individuals to enforce the ban, sets penalties up to 15% of a parent entity's revenue, and appropriates $1 billion to the FTC.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the companies that buy health and location data are better off so far: with the bill sitting untouched in committee, the current trade in sensitive data continues under existing law.

for.name: Bernie Sanders, Sheldon Whitehouse, and Ron Wyden
3 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 13, 2026 and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: Every senator attached to the bill is a Democrat or independent — 3 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents — with no Republican support in the record, and no action has been scheduled since referral.

industries.note: The bill's core target: companies like Acxiom that buy and resell information people never knowingly handed over would lose the legal ability to sell location and health data at all, and face lawsuits and penalties up to 15% of parent-entity revenue for violations.

industries.industry: Adtech and app companies selling location data
industries.note: Apps and location-analytics firms that monetize phone movements by feeding data to brokers would be barred from supplying them, cutting off a major revenue stream built on tracking people's whereabouts.

industries.industry: Health apps and AI chatbot companies
industries.note: The bill counts health questions typed into AI systems and health-app activity as health data, so companies that monetize what users reveal about pregnancies, medications, or mental health could no longer pass it to brokers — though HIPAA-compliant arrangements remain exempt.

analysis.trajectory: The Congress is still in session, but with only four cosponsors and no committee action since July 2026, the bill follows the familiar path of privacy legislation that dies quietly in committee. Unless the Commerce Committee schedules a hearing or the provisions are folded into a larger data privacy package, it will likely expire when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
